content: The means and standard deviations (SDs) of the four groups were combined for analysis. However, the SDs of the adjusted mean differences were not available in the published text. As a result, unadjusted values were used for the analysis. In the study by Oddy (2010), the percentage of children who were breastfed for varying durations was reported at the beginning of the study, along with the total number of subjects at the end of the study. It was assumed that the percentage of breastfeeding remained constant throughout, and the sample size (N) was derived from these figures. Owen (2002) provided cholesterol and LDL values in mmol/L. Novaes (2012) compared the risk of obesity in children breastfed for 6–11 months with those breastfed for more than 12 months. The group with more than 12 months of breastfeeding was used as the reference group (odds ratio [OR] = 1). The odds ratios were reversed for the purpose of analysis. Retnakumari (2012) extracted data from Figure 3 using the Automeris app. Rajaei (2016) also derived data using the Automeris WebPlotDigitizer app. Muniz (2015) presented data separately for men and women. These data were combined, and the SDs were calculated from the 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Harvey (2009) extracted data using the Automeris WebPlotDigitizer app. Martin (2002) similarly derived data using the Automeris WebPlotDigitizer app. Lima (2019) provided data as adjusted mean differences, with breastfeeding for ≥12 months used as the reference group (value = 0). The values were reversed for quantitative analysis, and biochemical values were converted to mmol/L for analysis. Izadi (2013) used Never Breastfed as the reference group (OR = 1). The odds ratio for continued breastfeeding (>12 months) versus breastfeeding for 7–12 months was imputed. Separate odds ratios for 12–18 months and 18–24 months of breastfeeding were provided and combined using generalized inverse variance (GIV) methods. Horta (2006) calculated SDs from 95% CIs. Means and CIs for males and females were provided separately and then combined. Hartwig (2019) used breastfeeding for 0–6 months as the reference group (relative risk [RR] = 1). The relative risk for continued breastfeeding (12–23 months) versus breastfeeding for 6–11 months was imputed. Duazo (2010) provided data for 5and 6-year-old children separately, along with the total number of subjects in the two groups. The number of subjects for various breastfeeding durations was reported as a combined group for both ages. It was assumed that the number of subjects for each age group was proportional to the total number provided. Camurdan (2011) reported BMI means and SDs separately for appropriate-for-gestational-age (AGA) and large-for-gestational-age (LGA) infants. These values were combined for quantitative analysis. Stordal (2017) presented data as adjusted relative risks (RRs), with breastfeeding for ≥12 months used as the reference group (RR = 1). The values were reversed for quantitative analysis. The RRs for upper and lower respiratory infections were combined using GIV methods to calculate the RRs for all respiratory tract infections. Nirunsittirat (2016) used breastfeeding for 0–6 months as the reference group (RR = 1). The relative risk for continued breastfeeding versus breastfeeding for 6–11 months was calculated. Separate RRs for 12–18 months and ≥18 months of breastfeeding were provided. The search terms included variations of infant, toddler, baby, child, mother, and women, among others, to ensure comprehensive coverage of relevant studies. The study flow diagram included the following outcomes: delayed development, underweight, stunting, BMI, BMI z-scores, obesity, overweight, infections (including gastrointestinal and respiratory tract infections), acute otitis media, dental caries, asthma, eczema, diabetes, blood glucose levels, hypertension, cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides, weight gain, waist circumference, breast cancer, ovarian cancer, osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease, and cardiovascular mortality. Specific subcategories, such as hypertension and dental caries at different breastfeeding durations, were also analyzed.
